newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grain - Soymeal prices continue rising.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Soymeal prices continue rising.

text.p: Soymeal prices continued to edge higher in Southeast Asia this week, reflecting high international quotes, particularly from India, and unsated local demand for imports, regional traders said on Wednesday.
Indonesian soymeal remained firm on tight supply and ahead of imports expected near term.
"Prices remain firm and are likely to stay so in the coming days despite the expected arrival of imported soymeal," one Jakarta-based trader said.
Soymeal was traded at 800-810 rupiah a kg in Surabaya against 790-800 rupiah last week and at 820-830 rupiah a kg in Jakarta versus the previous 815-820 rupiah, traders said.
Another dealer said the arrival of the imports was unlikely to have much impact on the local soymeal market as the shipments would mainly go straight to end-users, rather than traders.
"The imports are being done by the big feedmills, not by the traders, so the soymeal will go direct to their warehouses and not to the market," he said.
He added that Indonesian buyers recently bought between 70,000 to 90,000 tonnes of soymeal, from an undisclosed origin, for November/December shipment at $290-$304 a tonne C&F.
The trader said one local firm was also heard making bids at $314 a tonne C&F for 120,000 tonnes of Indian soymeal for November-March shipment, without giving further details.
On Monday, Singapore traders said Indonesia had bought around 20,000 to 25,000 tonnes of Indian new crop soymeal at about $320-$325 a tonne C&F for November to January shipment.
The Indonesian trader also said 80,000 tonnes of South American-origin soymeal was expected to arrive in the country between October to November, but price details were unavailable.
In Malaysia, soymeal was also quoted higher with domestic buyers seeking a further 20,000-tonne consignment after a recent purchase of 30,000 tonnes, traders said.

Local soymeal was trading up to 801.92 ringgit ($321) a tonne ex-factory/godown central region from 785.93 ringgit last week, they said. Imported soymeal had risen to about 780 ringgit a tonne from 760 ringgit.
"There is no acute shortage of meal in Malaysia," said a Singapore-based dealer. "We're only seeing demand at the lower level and nobody's rushing in to buy."
Another trader said he expected buyers to lock in orders if prices fell.
"Current meal prices, especially Indian soymeal, are almost at an all-time high," he said. Malaysian traders quoted Indian soymeal as high as $340 a tonne C&F for prompt delivery.

In Thailand, the price of locally crushed soymeal from imported beans firmed to 10.20 baht a kg from 10.05 last week, but traders expected the market to ease next month when imports from Brazil and Argentina arrive.

Thai feed millers recently ordered 36,000 tonnes of 44 percent protein soymeal from Argentina for prompt shipment. The price was said to be around $306-$307 a tonne C&F Bangkok, according to trade sources. They said the cargo was expected to arrive in mid-October.

But some local traders said they were staying out of the market this week on news the Thai government is considering lifting the import quota and reducing tariffs on certain animal feed ingredients, including soymeal, soybeans and corn.
Trends were mixed in the Southeast Asian corn market, with Indonesian prices slipping and those in Malaysia and Thailand on an upward tack.
Indonesian corn prices continued last week's fall due to supply pressure from the ongoing harvest in various corn growing regions in Sumatra, Java and Sulawesi, corn traders said.

High quality full yellow corn with a maximum of 16 percent water content was on offer at 420 rupiah a kg in Lampung against 455-460 rupiah last week. It was on offer at 450 rupiah/kg in Jakarta against 480-500 rupiah last week.
"Prices have fallen between five to 10 rupiah a kg almost every day since last week on an expected good harvest," one Jakarta-based trader said.
She said adequate rains in the main corn growing area of Lampung had produced a higher harvest, but could not give figures.
Confirmation was not available of market talk of corn imports from the United States and South Africa, but dealers said the rumours had further dampened market sentiment.
In Thailand, the price for benchmark 14.50 percent-moisture maize/corn paid by feed producers rose to around 4.50-4.60 baht a kg from 4.28-4.40 baht a week ago.
"It's the same old reason. Lots of maize was left dampened by rain in the farms. Little was transported to the market," one local trader said.
In Malaysia, bulk corn was quoted firmer at around 550 ringgit a tonne ex-factory/godown in the central region from 520 to 530 ringgit last week.
"A" grade wheat in bags was holding steady at 880 a tonne ex-factory/godown central region for the third week. Low-grade wheat was also trading at 550-600 ringgit as previously.
